tldr: Washington piled onto Nvidia over the weekend: Treasury Secretary Bessent called for an outside CEO and gave the board 10 days to answer on export compliance, while Jensen Huang agreed to closed-door testimony before 3 House committees.

The FT says Huang has discussed a comeback as allies lobby the board, and the NYT reports Lutnick pushed a narrower 7-country remote-access chip rule that overlaps with Cantor's business, two days before Nvidia's Nov 17 earnings.
Outside the Nvidia saga, a scan of 159,041 Lovable-built apps found 24,664 leaking database records without login; in China, Huawei Cloud put its openPangu-2.1-Pro flagship live on its MaaS platform.

items.title: Bessent says Nvidia needs a 'dramatic shakeup' and an outside CEO, wants board answers within 10 days
items.summary: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said on Fox News on Sunday that Nvidia's board should look outside the company for Jensen Huang's permanent successor, calling for a 'dramatic shakeup'. He said he wants the board and its outside counsel to answer within 10 days on export-control compliance and whether China sales were pushed to hit revenue targets. He did not say what would happen if they miss that deadline. The comments come two days before Nvidia's first earnings report under interim CEO Colette Kress.
items.why_it_matters: A sitting Treasury Secretary is publicly steering the CEO search at the world's most valuable chipmaker and setting it a compliance deadline. That raises the political stakes of the succession and of Nvidia's China business.

items.title: NYT: Lutnick pushed a narrower chip rule for overseas data centers that overlap with Cantor's business
items.summary: The New York Times reported on Sunday that Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick has argued for a narrower version of a pending rule on Chinese remote access to US AI chips in overseas data centers. His version would cover seven countries (Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia, Brazil, South Africa and Norway), apply only to future shipments, and require notification rather than a licence when Chinese customers train models there. Data centers already full of US hardware would be exempt. Cantor Fitzgerald, now run by Lutnick's sons, has done business with several Southeast Asian operators serving Chinese clients. The Times said it found no evidence that those dealings influenced his decisions.
items.why_it_matters: It ties a conflict-of-interest question to the specific export rule meant to close the Megaspeed-style remote-access loophole, which could weaken or delay the rule.

items.summary: The Financial Times reported on Sunday that Jensen Huang has discussed with confidants a possible return as Nvidia CEO, days after resigning. Allies are reportedly organising a Silicon Valley group to lobby the board and seek White House backing, and an associate told the FT that Huang supports the effort. Huang does not hold a controlling stake, so any return is up to the board. Nvidia says it has not engaged any candidate and calls the speculation premature.

items.title: Researchers find thousands of Lovable-built apps exposing passport data and 200,000+ chat messages
items.summary: Hamburg security firm Crissy Field, working with Handelsblatt, scanned 159,041 projects built on the Lovable vibe-coding platform and found user data readable without any login. Of the projects, 34,545 used Supabase and 24,664 returned database records with no authentication; one lifestyle forum exposed more than 200,000 chat messages and about 80,000 user profiles, and one service exposed more than 1,000 passport-related records. The cause was missing database access rules (row-level security) on Supabase tables, not a break-in. Lovable called it a known, industry-wide Supabase configuration problem.
items.why_it_matters: This is the largest measured sample so far of how AI-generated apps ship with insecure defaults. It also raises the question of who is responsible as Lovable moves from generating apps to hosting and running them.

learn.title: Mask the SFT loss to assistant tokens when tuning tool calling
learn.why_today: Huawei says openPangu-2.1-Pro's tool selection and calling were tuned on more than 100,000 specialised samples, which is supervised fine-tuning on multi-turn traces.
learn.explanation: A tool-use training example interleaves a system prompt with tool schemas, a user turn, the assistant's tool call, the tool's output and the final answer. Only the assistant spans are behaviour you want to teach, so the cross-entropy is averaged over those tokens and every other position gets a zero weight. Without the mask, most of the loss (and gradient) comes from predicting user text and tool outputs, which are noisy, long and not under the model's control, so the model learns to imitate tool responses instead of to call tools well. The mask also changes the normalisation: averaging over assistant tokens only means short tool calls are not drowned out by long tool outputs. It breaks down when the tool output itself must be parsed into structured state the model later relies on; some recipes then add a small weight on those tokens rather than zero.
learn.math: \mathcal{L} = -\frac{\sum_t m_t \log p_\theta(x_t\mid x_{<t})}{\sum_t m_t},\quad m_t = \mathbb{1}[\text{token } t \text{ is assistant-authored}]
learn.python:
import math
# Toy SFT example for tool calling: per-token log-probs the model assigns to the target token.
# Roles: S=system/tool schema, U=user, A=assistant (tool call + answer), T=tool output.
roles  = list("SSSSUUUUAAAATTTTTAAA")
logp   = [-0.1,-0.2,-0.1,-0.3, -2.0,-1.5,-2.2,-1.8, -0.9,-0.4,-0.2,-0.6,
          -3.0,-2.5,-2.8,-3.1,-2.9, -0.7,-0.5,-0.3]   # illustrative numbers
def nll(mask):
    picked = [-lp for lp, m in zip(logp, mask) if m]
    return sum(picked) / len(picked), len(picked)
full = nll([True] * len(roles))
asst = nll([r == "A" for r in roles])
print(f"loss on all tokens      : {full[0]:.3f} over {full[1]} tokens")
print(f"loss on assistant only  : {asst[0]:.3f} over {asst[1]} tokens")
# Gradient share: fraction of the summed loss that comes from tokens the model never has to produce
waste = sum(-lp for lp, r in zip(logp, roles) if r != "A") / sum(-lp for lp in logp)
print(f"share of unmasked loss from user/tool tokens: {waste:.0%}")

learn.title: Turn a Linpack exaflops figure into training days, and see why it misleads
learn.why_today: China's HPC TOP100 put the Lingsheng system first at 2.198 EFlops Linpack, a number often read as AI-training capacity.
learn.explanation: Training compute for a dense transformer is about C = 6ND FLOPs (N parameters, D tokens: 2ND forward, 4ND backward). Wall-clock time is C divided by sustained throughput, which is peak FLOP/s times model FLOPs utilisation (MFU, typically 30-50% at scale). Linpack Rmax is measured in FP64 on dense linear algebra, while training runs in BF16 or FP8, where accelerators can be an order of magnitude or more faster, so plugging Rmax in directly overstates training time; the uplift factor depends entirely on the hardware and is an assumption in the snippet. Interconnect bandwidth, memory capacity and failure rates then decide whether the MFU you assume is reachable, which is why HPL rank is a weak proxy for AI capacity. The numbers below are illustrative, not a claim about any real machine or model.
learn.python:
# Back-of-envelope: how long would a training run take on a machine of a given Linpack score?
# Illustrative model size and token count; HPL Rmax is FP64, AI training runs in BF16/FP8.
N = 1e12          # parameters (dense, illustrative)
D = 20e12         # training tokens (illustrative)
C = 6 * N * D     # training FLOPs, the 6ND rule for a dense transformer
rmax_fp64 = 2.198e18          # FLOP/s, Linpack Rmax quoted for the system
for label, peak in [("FP64 Rmax as-is", rmax_fp64),
                    ("x16 low-precision uplift (assumed)", rmax_fp64 * 16)]:
    for mfu in (0.3, 0.5):
        days = C / (peak * mfu) / 86400
        print(f"{label:36s} MFU={mfu:.0%}: {days:10.1f} days")
print(f"C = {C:.2e} FLOPs")
